output.brief: The gap is mostly a time-in-level effect, not proof of proximity bias. Remote hiring only opened in July 2024, so 215 of 340 remote staff started after March 2025. Only 32% of remote staff meet the policy's 18-month eligibility rule, against 74% of office staff. Among eligible people, nomination, approval and promotion rates are nearly identical: 20.0% remote against 21.1% office. Applying office rates to the remote eligibility mix predicts 8.2%, against 7.6% observed. Remote staff don't leave more often (10.9% against 11.6%), and the gap shows up in every job family, so job-family mix doesn't explain it. I'm fairly confident, though the eligible remote group is small (110), so a real difference of a few points can't be ruled out. Some visibility effects are plausible: managers hand urgent work to people sitting nearby, and remote staff are less likely to feel leaders know their work. We have no assignment data to test that. Don't announce the three-day office rule. It would penalise about 180 people hired on home-based contracts and rests on a misread comparison. Put it on hold. Report promotion rates for eligible staff only, and re-check at the FY2027 cycle. Also collect stretch-assignment data, and explain the promotion criteria to remote staff.
